predictions.claim: A typical cold player says the sound helped: the waterfall and seasonal creatures sit under the scene and the catch tock / cliche crumple mark the verbs.
A screen-reader player says the sound got in the way: the waterfall is broadband noise at 250 Hz to 2.4 kHz, the same band as synthesized speech, and it runs under every announcement.
Most players leave the sound on to the end; the ambience is quiet (about -34 dBFS) and nothing in play invites muting.
A screen-reader player turns sound off more often than a sighted one, because the Sound control is the first Tab stop and the waterfall masks speech.
The player ever touches the Sound control (to turn it off, or to answer 'Tap for sound' where the browser blocked the early start).
The player smashes a real cliche and hears the crumple with the announcement containing 'Snap', the one event where word and sound say the same thing.

notes: Events that deserve a sound and lack one: opening a phrase's choice (steps 3, 5, 7, 11, 17, 20, 28, 30) is silent and unannounced; focus lands on Catch line, but a soft lift of the paper (Snd.paper already exists) would say 'you picked this up'. Pause/Resume stream (steps 14, 15, 25, 26, 40, 41) and Show turn marks (16, 27, 42) change state with no sound and no announcement; pausing the stream is the one place where the waterfall itself could carry the meaning (duck it while paused, restore on resume), which is Murch's worldizing: the pond's own water tells you the stream has stopped. Move to top/bottom (9, 10, 22, 23) and Remove (13, 24, 39) are announced but silent; a tock variant pitched by line would pair with the words (XAG 103) without carrying the meaning alone (XAG 104).

Let it go (steps 12, 33) calls Snd.swish() in code, but Layer 1 heard no sound: a .09-peak bandpassed noise under a running waterfall of the same texture is masked. The one exit verb is effectively silent; it needs a pitched or panned element (a receding downstream swish, panned off) to separate from the bed.

Competition with reading: the waterfall body (highpass 250, lowpass 2400) occupies the speech band for the whole session; suggest ducking the bed about 6 dB for the length of each live-region announcement. The summer minminzemi (sawtooth, 0.12 peak, filtered near 1.9 kHz, about 5 s long) is the loudest creature and lands squarely on speech; it will collide with announcements in round 2. The yaa (0.55 peak, the loudest sound in the build) is earned, since it is the kireji moment, but it should not fire under a live announcement.

Step 32: a tile tap produced 8 short sounds with nothing announced. Either a seasonal creature (uguisu, 4 whistles plus overtones) happened to coincide or a play sound fired unannounced; if the latter it is a sound carrying information alone (XAG 104). Worth one re-crawl with creatures disabled to separate bed from events.

halts.check: E1 GESTURE-FIRST: sound before the first tap (founder rules)
halts.evidence: Line 2126 calls Snd.wake() at load ('where the browser allows it, sound starts before any touch at all'); Layer 1 measured the waterfall at -36.2 dBFS before any touch. Against: studio OS section 2 says the first tap unlocks audio, permission-clean and ambush-free, and for a screen-reader player an unasked noise bed arrives before the first spoken word. For: the level is low, fades in over about 1.5 s, the mute is the first Tab stop and drops output to -85.5 dBFS (WCAG 1.4.2 is met: a stop mechanism exists at the top), the choice persists in localStorage, and the pond being already alive is the scene-first opening the studio also asks for. The code path conflicts with a stated law, so it is filed as blocking; the founder decides whether the law or the scene wins, or whether a middle path (bed starts on the first tap anywhere, which the capture listeners already do) is enough.
